title: A Soccer Star Is Stuck in Jail for a Speeding Ticket?
summary:
Imagine being a professional soccer player who has played in four countries, and then getting stuck in jail for months because of a traffic stop! That's what happened to Homero Calderón, a dad from Venezuela. He has two little kids who were born in the U.S., ages 1 and 3.

Calderón was driving to a car shop in Florida in late February when police pulled him over for speeding. They arrested him for driving without a valid Florida license, even though his wife says he had an international driving permit. Then he was handed over to ICE—that's Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the agency that deals with people who might be in the country illegally.

Now he's been in a detention center in Georgia for almost six months. His wife, Daniela Molina, says he's feeling really down. "I've been 17 years with Homero," she said in a video. "I had never heard him cry or ask for help like he has." He even missed his daughter's first birthday.

Here's the tricky part: Calderón had already applied to stay in the U.S. legally. He asked for an extension of his tourist visa and also applied for a special visa for people with extraordinary abilities—like being a great soccer player. But those applications are still waiting to be processed. The government says he overstayed his permission, but his lawyers say he was doing everything right.

There are over 11 million immigration cases waiting to be processed right now. That's a huge backlog! Some experts say the government is taking so long on purpose, so they can arrest people who are waiting. Calderón's case shows how even people who follow the rules can get caught in the system.
why_it_matters: This story shows how confusing rules and long waits can separate a family, which can feel unfair and scary for kids, including Calderón's own young children.

In the U.S., immigration officials can detain people while their visa cases are decided, which sometimes takes months or years.
A visa is permission to be in a country, and different visas exist for tourists, workers, and people with special talents.

WHAT: He was arrested at a traffic stop for driving without a valid Florida license, handed over to ICE, and has been held in a detention center for almost six months.
WHERE: He was pulled over in Florida and is now detained in Georgia.
WHY: His family says he had an international driving permit and applied to stay legally, but the government says he overstayed while his applications are stuck in a huge backlog.
